new.title: See Dufy's electricity mural at the Musée d'Art Moderne
new.desc: The city's modern art museum fills the east wing of the Palais de Tokyo, built for the 1937 World's Fair. Its permanent collection is free and includes monumental murals by Raoul Dufy and Henri Matisse, among them Dufy's vast La Fée Électricité.
new.tip: The terrace between the two wings of the Palais de Tokyo looks over the Seine towards the Eiffel Tower, a good spot for a break between galleries.
new.q: Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris, 11 avenue du Président Wilson, Paris

new.title: Travel through Asia at the Musée Guimet
new.desc: Lyon industrialist Émile Guimet founded this museum in 1879 and moved it to Place d'Iéna in 1889. It is one of the great collections of Asian art outside Asia, with an outstanding gallery of Khmer sculpture from Cambodia.
new.tip: Leave time for the Panthéon Bouddhique wing a short walk up avenue d'Iéna, a quieter space devoted to Buddhist art.

new.title: Walk past cathedral portals at the Cité de l'architecture
new.desc: In the Palais de Chaillot, full-size plaster casts of French cathedral portals and sculpture from the 12th to the 18th century fill a huge gallery. Another floor has copies of Romanesque and Gothic murals and stained glass, so you can study church art at eye level.
new.tip: Come on a weekday morning, when you may have the vast cast gallery almost to yourself.
new.q: Cité de l'architecture et du patrimoine, 1 place du Trocadéro, Paris

new.title: Visit Balzac's hideaway in Passy
new.desc: Balzac rented the top floor of this little house from 1840 to 1847, partly to hide from his creditors, and here he edited La Comédie humaine and wrote La Cousine Bette. Entry to the house and its garden is free; only temporary exhibitions are paid.
new.tip: Sit for a while in the garden, then walk round to cobbled rue Berton below, one of the most village-like lanes left in Paris.
new.q: Maison de Balzac, 47 rue Raynouard, Paris

new.title: Admire the modernist villas of rue Mallet-Stevens
new.desc: This short dead-end street in Auteuil was opened in 1927 and lined with white reinforced-concrete houses by Robert Mallet-Stevens, who lived and had his office at number 12. Number 10 was the house-studio of the sculptor twins Jan and Joël Martel.
new.tip: The houses are private, so admire them from the pavement. Le Corbusier's Maison La Roche is a two-minute walk away on square du Docteur-Blanche.

new.title: Find the royal chapel hidden in square Louis-XVI
new.desc: Fontaine's neoclassical chapel, built between 1816 and 1826, stands on the old Madeleine cemetery where Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were first buried after the guillotine. Symbolic tombs around the cloister honour the Swiss Guards killed defending the royal family in August 1792.
new.tip: The garden around it is a calm lunch spot near Saint-Lazare. The chapel itself is run by the Centre des monuments nationaux and charges a small fee.

new.title: Stand under the glass roof of the Grand Palais
new.desc: Built for the 1900 World's Fair, the Grand Palais has a nave about 200 metres long under some 14,000 square metres of iron and glass. After a four-year restoration it fully reopened in June 2025 with new galleries, a new public entrance and a children's area.
new.tip: The nave is used for exhibitions, fairs and events rather than open all the time, so check what is on and book. Afterwards cross Pont Alexandre III for the view towards the Invalides.

new.title: Light a candle in the Russian cathedral on rue Daru
new.desc: Consecrated in 1861, the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral brought gilded onion domes and a Byzantine interior to the 8th arrondissement. Picasso married the dancer Olga Khokhlova here in 1918, with Cocteau, Max Jacob and Apollinaire as witnesses.
new.tip: Drop in during part of a Sunday morning liturgy to hear the unaccompanied choir, and dress modestly. Parc Monceau is a short walk away.

new.title: Meet the giant Buddha of the Musée Cernuschi
new.desc: Banker Henri Cernuschi left his mansion beside Parc Monceau and his Asian art collection to the city, and it opened as a museum in 1898. The star is a large 18th-century Japanese bronze Buddha from Meguro, which dominates the main hall.
new.tip: The permanent collection is free. Reach it along avenue Vélasquez, the gated lane between boulevard Malesherbes and Parc Monceau.

new.title: Visit Manet and Debussy in the Passy cemetery
new.desc: Opened in 1820 behind the Trocadéro, this small terraced cemetery holds Édouard Manet, Berthe Morisot, Claude Debussy, Gabriel Fauré and the actor Fernandel. It sits right in the shadow of the Eiffel Tower.
new.tip: Look for the tomb Manet shares with Berthe Morisot, who married his brother Eugène. Pair it with the Trocadéro gardens just below.

new.title: Step onto the loggia of the Hôtel de la Marine
new.desc: Ange-Jacques Gabriel's palace on Place de la Concorde was built between 1757 and 1774 for the royal furniture store, then housed the French Navy from 1789 until 2015. Restored and opened to visitors in 2021, it shows gilded 18th-century apartments and a colonnaded loggia over the square.
new.tip: Make sure your visit includes the loggia, from where you look over the obelisk to the Assemblée nationale across the river.
new.q: Hôtel de la Marine, 2 place de la Concorde, Paris

new.title: Dine among the mosaics of Brasserie Mollard
new.desc: Opposite Gare Saint-Lazare, this brasserie was redecorated in 1895 by architect Édouard-Jean Niermans with Sarreguemines ceramics and mosaics showing life around the station. The décor was hidden behind paint and mirrors after the First World War, rediscovered in 1965 and listed as a historic monument in 1989.
new.tip: Ask for a table in the main room under the ceramic panels. Seafood platters are the house speciality, and it is handy before a late train.

new.title: Have dinner where the Paris jam session was born
new.desc: Le Bœuf sur le Toit opened in 1921 as a bar named after a Darius Milhaud ballet, and Jean Cocteau's circle made it the hub of jazz-age Paris. Musicians jammed here so often that the French phrase for a jam session, faire un bœuf, is said to come from its name. It has been on rue du Colisée since 1941.
new.tip: Today it is a brasserie and music hall with a Cocteau-inspired ceiling fresco; pick an evening with live music.
new.q: Le Bœuf sur le Toit, 34 rue du Colisée, Paris

new.title: Shop at the covered market of the Batignolles
new.desc: Between rue Lemercier and rue des Moines, this modest covered hall is where the Batignolles does its daily shopping: cheese, fish, meat, charcuterie, wine, bread and traiteurs under one roof. It has a real village feel, far from the tourist trail.
new.tip: It opens Tuesday to Sunday, all day on Saturday. Take your picnic to the Square des Batignolles a few minutes away.
new.q: Marché couvert des Batignolles, 96 bis rue Lemercier, Paris

new.title: Taste raw fish at the Marché couvert de Passy
new.desc: Just off Place de Passy, this elegant covered market is used mostly by locals for its fishmonger, cheese shop, greengrocers and caterers. The family fishmonger, a fixture for decades, has added a counter serving raw fish prepared on the spot.
new.tip: Mornings are liveliest, and it is closed on Mondays. Afterwards stroll down rue de Passy towards the Jardin du Ranelagh.
new.q: Marché couvert de Passy, 1 rue Bois-le-Vent, Paris

new.title: Graze along rue Poncelet near Place des Ternes
new.desc: Rue Poncelet and its corner with rue Bayen form one of the best market streets in Paris, with bakeries, fishmongers, butchers and greengrocers whose stalls spill onto the pavement. At number 13, Alléosse ages its cheeses in its own cellars and is a reference for Paris cheese lovers.
new.tip: Come on a Saturday morning for the full bustle. Shops close on Mondays and on Sunday afternoons.

new.title: Treat yourself at La Grande Cascade in the Bois
new.desc: At the foot of the artificial waterfall in the Bois de Boulogne, this former rest pavilion of Napoleon III became a restaurant during the 1900 World's Fair. It keeps its Belle Époque dining room and holds a Michelin star for classic French cooking.
new.tip: Book ahead and aim for a summer lunch on the terrace under its big canopy. Then walk over to the Grande Cascade itself and its rocky grotto.
new.q: La Grande Cascade, allée de Longchamp, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

new.title: Order oysters at Le Stella on avenue Victor-Hugo
new.desc: This old-school brasserie on the corner of rue de la Pompe has been a 16th arrondissement fixture for generations, with a mid-century dining room. Its oyster bar is the draw, alongside brasserie classics such as andouillette and calf's liver.
new.tip: It is open every day until late, which makes it a reliable choice on a Sunday evening when many neighbourhood places are shut.
new.q: Le Stella, 133 avenue Victor Hugo, Paris

new.title: Dine facing the Eiffel Tower at the Café de l'Homme
new.desc: Inside the Palais de Chaillot, next to the Musée de l'Homme, this restaurant has a large terrace looking straight across the Seine at the Eiffel Tower. The menu is modern French with plenty of seafood.
new.tip: Book a terrace table for dinner and stay for the tower's sparkle, which runs for a few minutes on the hour after dark.
new.q: Café de l'Homme, 17 place du Trocadéro, Paris

new.title: Share a seafood platter at La Lorraine
new.desc: Open on Place des Ternes since 1919, La Lorraine is one of the big brasseries of western Paris, redone in Art Deco spirit by designer Laura Gonzalez. It is known for oysters, langoustines, crab and lobster, alongside brasserie classics.
new.tip: It serves from breakfast to late every day, and the big south-facing terrace on the square catches the sun.
new.q: La Lorraine, 2 place des Ternes, Paris

new.title: Take a Bateaux-Mouches cruise from Pont de l'Alma
new.desc: The big open-deck boats of the Compagnie des Bateaux-Mouches leave from the quay by Pont de l'Alma for a cruise of about an hour past the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre and Notre-Dame. The name comes from the Mouche district of Lyon, where the first boats were built.
new.tip: Take an evening departure: once night falls the boats' floodlights sweep across the facades along the quays.
new.q: Bateaux-Mouches, Port de la Conférence, Paris

new.title: Hear a concert at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées
new.desc: Built in 1913 by the Perret brothers with reliefs by Antoine Bourdelle, this was the first Art Deco building in Paris, and two months after opening it hosted the riotous premiere of Stravinsky's Rite of Spring. Today it stages opera and a big concert season with leading orchestras.
new.tip: The cheapest seats high up sell out first but still give a fine view of the painted dome.
new.q: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, 15 avenue Montaigne, Paris

new.title: Go behind the scenes at Roland-Garros
new.desc: The home of the French Open was built in 1928 and named after a pioneering aviator killed in the First World War. Guided tours take you through the players' areas to the edge of Court Philippe-Chatrier and include the Tenniseum, the tennis museum.
new.tip: Tours pause during the tournament in late May and early June, when you need a match ticket instead. The nearest métro is Porte d'Auteuil.

new.title: Dress up for the Prix de l'Arc at Longchamp
new.desc: Opened in 1857 in the Bois de Boulogne, the Longchamp racecourse hosts France's most prestigious horse race, the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, every October. It reopened in 2018 with a long, sleek grandstand by Dominique Perrault.
new.tip: Book Arc weekend tickets early. Ordinary race days through the season are far cheaper and calmer, a good way to try the races.

new.title: Watch an open-air play in the Jardin Shakespeare
new.desc: Inside the Pré Catelan garden in the Bois de Boulogne, this garden was replanted in 1952 with scenes from Shakespeare's plays, from Ophelia's willow and pond to a Scottish moor for Macbeth. From late May to late September its open-air theatre stages around 90 plays, concerts and readings.
new.tip: Bring a sweater for evening shows and check the programme: some events are free, plays cost from about 15 euros. Bus 244 stops nearby.
new.q: Théâtre de Verdure du Jardin Shakespeare, Pré Catelan, Bois de Boulogne, Paris

new.title: Watch the Bastille Day parade on the Champs-Élysées
new.desc: On the morning of 14 July, troops march down the Champs-Élysées from the Arc de Triomphe to Place de la Concorde in one of the oldest regular military parades in the world, held almost every year since 1880. The Patrouille de France leads the flypast overhead.
new.tip: Arrive very early for a place at the barriers, and bring water and a hat. Even from further back, the flypast is visible from anywhere along the avenue.

new.title: Feel the noise of a PSG match at the Parc des Princes
new.desc: Paris Saint-Germain have played in Roger Taillibert's concrete bowl since 1974. The stadium opened in 1972 on the site of an 1897 cycling velodrome where the Tour de France finished for decades, and its steep stands of nearly 48,000 seats keep the crowd close to the pitch.
new.tip: Buy tickets only through the club's official channels, and get in early to hear the Auteuil and Boulogne ends start their chants.
new.q: Parc des Princes, 24 rue du Commandant Guilbaud, Paris

new.title: Browse old stamps and postcards at the Marché aux Timbres
new.desc: At the corner of avenue de Marigny and avenue Gabriel, just off the Champs-Élysées, dealers and private collectors set up open-air tables of stamps, postcards and old letters. It runs on Thursdays, weekends and public holidays.
new.tip: Even if you do not collect, a few euros buys a vintage Paris postcard. Champs-Élysées Clemenceau métro is a short walk away.
new.q: Marché aux timbres, avenue de Marigny, Paris

new.title: Face the flayed horseman at the Musée Fragonard
new.desc: Founded in 1766 at the veterinary school of Alfort, this cabinet of curiosities holds skeletons, organs and about twenty 18th-century écorchés by Honoré Fragonard, real bodies preserved and posed. The most famous is a flayed man riding a galloping horse.
new.tip: It opens on Wednesday, Thursday and weekend afternoons and is free for under 26s. Métro line 8 to École Vétérinaire de Maisons-Alfort stops by the gate. Not for the squeamish.
new.q: Musée Fragonard, 7 avenue du Général de Gaulle, Maisons-Alfort

new.title: Walk under the aqueduct of Arcueil
new.desc: A stone bridge 379 metres long and nearly 19 metres high carries the Médicis aqueduct across the Bièvre valley between Arcueil and Cachan. Built between 1613 and 1623 for Marie de Médicis, it was later topped with the arches of the Vanne aqueduct, which still brings water to Paris.
new.tip: Take RER B to Arcueil-Cachan or Laplace and follow the arches on foot; they look most impressive from the valley floor.

new.title: Explore the star-shaped housing of Ivry
new.desc: Between 1969 and 1975 architects Jean Renaudie and Renée Gailhoustet rebuilt the centre of Ivry-sur-Seine as a cluster of concrete buildings with pointed, planted terraces that look like stars from above. It is one of the boldest experiments in French social housing.
new.tip: People live here, so stay discreet. Val-de-Marne Tourisme runs occasional guided walks; otherwise start from Mairie d'Ivry on métro line 7.

new.title: See the last Baltard pavilion of Les Halles in Nogent
new.desc: When the iron and glass market halls of Les Halles were demolished, one of Victor Baltard's pavilions was taken apart and rebuilt in Nogent-sur-Marne in the 1970s. It is now a concert and events hall housing a Christie cinema organ built for the Gaumont-Palace.
new.tip: The inside opens only for events and on European Heritage Days in September, but the outside can be admired any time on the way down to the Marne.
new.q: Pavillon Baltard, 12 avenue Victor Hugo, Nogent-sur-Marne

new.title: Follow the Axe Majeur down to the Oise
new.desc: Artist Dani Karavan worked for over thirty years on this 3.2 km line of twelve stations in Cergy, from a 36-metre tilted tower past twelve white columns to an esplanade looking towards La Défense and Paris. Steps and slopes then drop to the ponds and a red footbridge over the Oise.
new.tip: Take RER A to Cergy-Saint-Christophe; the esplanade and its columns are a short walk from the station.

new.title: Climb inside the cliff at La Roche-Guyon
new.desc: In one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France, this château grew from a 12th-century castle dug into the cliff above the Seine into an elegant La Rochefoucauld residence. In 1944 it was Rommel's headquarters during the battle of Normandy.
new.tip: Climb the stairs cut through the rock up to the medieval keep for the view over the Seine, then visit the restored fruit and vegetable garden.

new.title: Step into Doctor Gachet's house in Auvers
new.desc: Dr Paul Gachet, doctor, amateur painter and collector, bought this house in 1872 and welcomed Pissarro, Cézanne and, in 1890, Van Gogh, who painted him three times. The salon is set out as it was in 1890, and the terraced garden is the one Van Gogh painted.
new.tip: It opens from spring to early November, Wednesday to Sunday, and entry costs just a few euros. Wear sturdy shoes for the steep garden steps.
new.q: Maison du Docteur Gachet, 78 rue du Docteur Gachet, Auvers-sur-Oise

new.title: Step into Impressionism at the Château d'Auvers
new.desc: Built in 1635 for an Italian banker from Marie de Médicis's circle, this château above Auvers-sur-Oise has French gardens redrawn from old engravings. Inside, the permanent show Vision impressionniste uses projections to immerse you in the world of the Impressionists.
new.tip: Check opening times before you go, as hours are seasonal. The terraced gardens look out over the village Van Gogh painted.
new.q: Château d'Auvers, rue de Léry, Auvers-sur-Oise

new.title: Find contemporary art in a medieval abbey
new.desc: Queen Blanche of Castile founded Maubuisson for Cistercian nuns in the 1230s. The chapter house, the latrine building with its water channel and a 13th-century tithe barn survive, and since 2001 they have hosted contemporary art exhibitions.
new.tip: Leave time to walk around the park and its pond, fed by the Ru de Liesse.

new.title: See Pissarro's Pontoise at the Musée Pissarro
new.desc: Perched on the old castle site at the top of the ramparts above the Oise, this small museum shows Camille Pissarro, his sons and fellow landscape painters such as Daubigny, Signac and Caillebotte, in works from about 1860 to 1910. Pissarro lived and painted in Pontoise for years.
new.tip: Step out to the garden in front of the museum for the view over the Oise valley that the painters knew.
new.q: Musée Pissarro, 17 rue du Château, Pontoise

new.title: Wander the world gardens of the Musée Albert-Kahn
new.desc: Banker Albert Kahn sent photographers around the globe between 1909 and 1931, and his Archives of the Planet hold some 72,000 colour autochromes. His 3.9-hectare garden in Boulogne mixes Japanese, French and English scenes with a Vosges forest, and the museum reopened in 2022 with a new building by Kengo Kuma.
new.tip: Come in spring when the Japanese garden is in flower. Boulogne Pont de Saint-Cloud on métro line 10 is a short walk away.
new.q: Musée Albert-Kahn, 2 rue du Port, Boulogne-Billancourt

new.title: Visit Joséphine's Château de Malmaison
new.desc: Joséphine bought this country house west of Paris in 1799 while Napoleon was in Egypt and filled its grounds with roses and exotic animals. It was the seat of government from 1800 to 1802, Napoleon stayed here briefly before his exile in 1815, and it has been a Napoleonic museum since 1905.
new.tip: Check what is on in the park as well as the house: the grounds keep a rose garden in memory of Joséphine's famous collection.

new.title: Line up the Grande Arche with the Arc de Triomphe
new.desc: Johan Otto von Spreckelsen's hollow cube, about 110 metres on each side, was inaugurated on 14 July 1989 at the end of the historic axis that runs from the Louvre through the Arc de Triomphe. It is turned 6.33 degrees because a station and a motorway lie under its foundations.
new.tip: Stand at the top of the great steps and look back down the axis towards the Arc de Triomphe, about 4 km away.

new.title: Picnic under the cherry blossom in the Parc de Sceaux
new.desc: André Le Nôtre laid out this 181-hectare park for Colbert, with a 1,140-metre Grand Canal, cascades with masks by Rodin and a château that is now a museum. In early spring its grove of Japanese cherry trees draws crowds for hanami picnics.
new.tip: Bloom is short and depends on the weather, usually late March to mid April; go on a weekday morning to avoid the crowds. RER B to Parc de Sceaux or Bourg-la-Reine.

new.title: Look over Paris from the Parc de Saint-Cloud
new.desc: This 460-hectare national estate was the site of a royal and imperial château that burned in 1870. Its Le Nôtre gardens, English landscape park and Marie-Antoinette's rose garden remain, and the Lanterne viewpoint takes in the Paris skyline.
new.tip: Come at the end of the day for the light on the city. The Pont de Sèvres and Boulogne Pont de Saint-Cloud métro stations are close to the park gates.

new.title: Catch a concert on the island at La Seine Musicale
new.desc: On Île Seguin in the Seine at Boulogne, Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines designed this music centre, opened in 2017, with an egg-shaped auditorium for 1,150 people under a moving sail of solar panels. The larger Grande Seine hall hosts pop concerts and shows.
new.tip: Arrive early and walk around the island before the show to see the river on both sides.
new.q: La Seine Musicale, Île Seguin, Boulogne-Billancourt

new.title: Drink a Gallia at the brewery bar in Pantin
new.desc: Gallia was founded in Paris in 1890 and by 1896 was the biggest brewery in the capital, before disappearing in the 1960s. Revived, it has brewed in a former boilermaking workshop in Pantin since 2015, and its bar at 35 rue Méhul pours beer from the brewery next door.
new.tip: Guided brewery tours with a tasting run regularly; book ahead. The bar hosts concerts and DJ sets, and Église de Pantin métro is a short walk away.

new.title: Shop at the Marché des Quatre-Routes
new.desc: Held three mornings a week in La Courneuve, this is counted among the largest markets in the Paris region, known for its variety and low prices. Since 2019 it has had a 3,000 square metre covered hall on Place Claire-Lacombe.
new.tip: It runs on Tuesday, Friday and Sunday mornings until about 1pm. Bring cash and a big bag; métro line 7 to La Courneuve 8 Mai 1945.
new.q: Marché des Quatre-Routes, place Claire-Lacombe, La Courneuve

new.title: Tour the Rungis wholesale market at dawn
new.desc: When Les Halles left central Paris in 1969, the city's food market moved to Rungis, now a 232-hectare town of pavilions for fish, meat, cheese, fruit, vegetables and flowers. It is closed to the public, but guided tours open the doors in the small hours, with tastings along the way.
new.tip: Public tours usually run on the first Friday of the month and start around 4am; book well ahead through the market's official site.

new.title: See a match at the Stade de France
new.desc: France's national stadium opened in 1998 and hosted that year's World Cup final, when France beat Brazil 3 to 0. Its 81,000 seats sit under a 13,000-tonne elliptical roof, and it staged athletics and the closing ceremonies of the 2024 Olympics.
new.tip: A Six Nations rugby match in late winter gives a great atmosphere. Use RER D to Stade de France Saint-Denis or RER B to La Plaine Stade de France.

new.title: Catch a film at Le Méliès in Montreuil
new.desc: Named after film pioneer Georges Méliès, who built his studio in Montreuil, this public cinema moved into a six-screen building in 2015 and is billed as the largest art-house cinema in Europe. Tickets cost a fraction of Paris prices.
new.tip: Check the programme for screenings with directors, and eat at its bar-restaurant. Métro Mairie de Montreuil is right outside.

new.title: Swim in the Marne at Joinville-le-Pont
new.desc: Supervised swimming has returned to the Marne at a few summer sites. At Joinville-le-Pont, a sandbank by the marina becomes a beach with separate pools for adults and children, lifeguards and free sunbeds.
new.tip: It usually opens from late June to the end of August. Book a slot online a few days ahead, and note it can close if water quality drops; swimming elsewhere in the river is banned.

new.title: Get lost in Parc Georges-Valbon
new.desc: At 417 hectares, this landscaped park around La Courneuve is the third-largest green space in the Paris region, with hills, viewpoints, 12-metre cascades and seven lakes. Most of it is a Natura 2000 site for birds, and it hosted the Fête de l'Humanité for decades.
new.tip: Start at the Grand Lac and climb one of the belvedere hills. Several entrances are close to the T11 tram.

new.title: Ride the whitewater course at the Cergy leisure island
new.desc: On a bend of the Oise, this 250-hectare leisure park has six lakes fed by groundwater, a supervised sandy beach, a cable waterski tow, a surf wave and an artificial whitewater course for rafting and kayaking.
new.tip: Come on a weekday to avoid the summer weekend crowds, and book rafting sessions in advance.
new.q: Île de loisirs de Cergy-Pontoise, Cergy
